title: CBA ad boost injects hope into local media
full_text:
Commonwealth Bank of Australia will increase its advertising and marketing investment in Australian media organisations by 40 per cent over the next two financial years, in a multimillion-dollar commitment that could provide a significant boost to the embattled local media industry.
The move by one of Australia’s biggest advertisers follows a series of trials which the bank says demonstrates that partnerships with local media delivers stronger commercial outcomes, challenging the dominance of global technology platforms in corporate advertising budgets.
The commitment comes as Australian media companies step up appeals to brands and marketers to reconsider advertising allocations, with an estimated 75c in every dollar currently directed towards digital channels, the majority of which flow overseas to global technology platforms.
The shift towards companies such as Meta, Google and TikTok has intensified pressure on Australian media organisations, which are left to fight over the minority share of the advertising revenue allocated to local media companies.
CBA said the decision was backed by its own research which showed advertising partnerships with news brands delivered “substantially higher” results, including stronger consumer intent and consideration, than campaigns appearing on non-news sites.
The bank also believes investment in local media can improve its visibility in AI-generated responses, as consumers increasingly turn to large language models for brand and product comparisons.
The increased investment will be funded by reallocating budgets from other areas, with much of the spending directed towards partnership content. While the bank will continue working with established Australian media organisations, it will also expand opportunities to invest in smaller independent publishers and content creators.
The decision is the result of 18 months of experimentation, according to CommBank’s in-house media and creative agency CBAgency managing director Pat Crowley.
“The economic model that funds Australian journalism has changed but the need for trusted news and information has not,” he said.
“The pressure on the sector came from a shift in the commercial settings of the new economy, and businesses that advertise are a critical part of that economy.” Mr Crowley said the bank had been exploring “deeper partnerships with local media”, with the results delivering “stronger commercial outcomes” for the business.
The commercial results are particularly significant given that advertising effectiveness remains the principal argument used by marketers and agencies to justify their existing media allocations.
It also comes as brands grapple with rising digital advertising costs, increasing ad loads and growing consumer fatigue, prompting renewed scrutiny of the returns delivered by established digital channels. Mr Crowley said CBA’s decision was also part of the bank’s commitment to supporting its customers.
“A diverse and trusted local media sector is central to a healthy democracy,” he said. “Australian businesses can play an important role in assisting with the sustainability of local media.” The bank is also hoping its decision will encourage other major advertisers to direct more of their budgets towards Australian media organisations, particularly smaller independent operations.
The issue of brands’ responsibility in supporting local media has intensified since Meta and Google withdrew from the News Media Bargaining Code, with publishers increasingly warning that the migration of advertising dollars to global technology platforms threatens the sustainability of local journalism.
The debate was front and centre at this year’s media upfronts, where media organisations showcase new products and programming in an effort to attract advertising budgets.
Nine and Seven both called on marketers to increase their investment in Australian media, while independent media company Mamamia urged brands to reconsider their spending with foreign-owned platforms.
Mamamia founder Mia Freedman told audiences: “Every single media business in Australia is under threat right now.” She also criticised the societal impact of the foreign-owned technology platforms.
“They’re radicalising young men. They’re funnelling boys directly into the manosphere. They’re impacting the mental health of entire generations of girls and young women in the most devastating ways,” she said.
“Our homegrown media brands and audiences have earned the right to be a bigger part of your mix.
“Not as a favour and not because we want you to take a risk. But because homegrown media is effective.” Despite growing calls for more spending in Australian media, there remains little consensus on how to achieve that shift, with proposals for both voluntary and mandatory investment commitments continuing to face resistance.
Last month CBA signed a landmark copyright deal which saw it become the first corporate heavyweight to pay Australian creators and publishers for the use of their content in workplace generative AI tools.
The deal, inked with the not-for-profit Copyright Agency, will mean any of CBA’s more than 50,000 employees can use local media content in prompts, summaries and content created for and by workplace AI tools. The licence fees will be paid to the creators and publishers to support the ongoing investment in local media content.
